findings.headline: Section 151 officer assessed low risk of Section 114 insolvency notice in short to medium term, conditional on continued budget discipline
findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer confirmed low risk that a Section 114 notice (declaration of insolvency or threatened insolvency) would be needed in the short to medium term. However this assessment explicitly depends on the council continuing to pass a balanced budget by 11 March each year. If this budget discipline lapses, the assessment would no longer hold.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice signals serious financial distress; low risk is positive, but the conditional nature indicates the council has limited buffer before insolvency risk crystallises.
findings.figures: Low Section 114 risk assessed; conditional on balanced budgets
findings.quote: The Section 151 officer confirms that based on the information currently available, there is a low risk of a Section 114 notice needing to be issued in the short to medium term, provided at all times that the Council continues to pass a balanced budget by the 11th of March each year.

findings.headline: Auditor General issued unqualified opinion with no material uncertainties affecting going concern
findings.detail: The Auditor General for Wales completed the audit without qualification. The auditor confirmed no material uncertainties exist that could cast significant doubt on the council's ability to continue as a going concern for at least 12 months from year-end. No exceptions were reported on audit access, accounting records, or agreement with records.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on independent audit assurance; an unqualified opinion with no going concern uncertainties confirms the financial position is fairly stated and sustainable.
findings.figures: Unqualified audit opinion; no material going concern uncertainties identified
findings.quote: Based on the work I have performed, I have not identified any material uncertainties relating to events or conditions that, individually or collectively, may cast significant doubt on Ceredigion County Council's ability to continue to adopt the going concern basis of accounting for a period of at least 12 months from when the financial statements are authorised for issue.

findings.headline: General Balances at £7.3m represent 3.3% of budget, positioned at the minimum of the council's 3-5% target range
findings.detail: Year-end General Balances of £7.3m stand at 3.3% of the 26/27 budget, at the lower edge of the council's target range. Combined with £44.4m Earmarked Reserves, total usable reserves provide approximately 85 days of financial cover against a £221m budget. This leaves limited headroom for further deterioration before the council breaches its reserves policy.
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial resilience; reserves at the minimum of target range leave little room for unforeseen events without policy breach.
findings.figures: £7.3m General Balances; 3.3% of 26/27 budget; target range 3-5%; £44.4m Earmarked Reserves; 85 days cover
findings.quote: The final position results in the Council's General Balances ending the year at £7.3m, equating to 3.3% of the 26/27 Budget. This is an important metric as the Council aims to keep within a target range of 3% and 5%

findings.headline: Revenue budget balanced with only £278k (0.13%) underspend, providing minimal margin for variation
findings.detail: The council delivered a final revenue outturn of £278k underspend against £209.2m budget. While demonstrating tight financial control, the 0.13% variance indicates the council has very little buffer; any unexpected change in the final quarter could have produced break-even or overspend.
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial flexibility; a 0.13% margin suggests the council is managing with minimal headroom for surprises.
findings.figures: £278k underspend; £209.2m budget; 0.13% variance
findings.quote: The final overall revenue outturn position for 25/26 is an improved underspend of £278k, against a 25/26 Budget of £209.2m. This equates to a variance of 0.13%

findings.headline: Through Age & Wellbeing services held overspend to £154k (0.23%) despite ongoing demand pressures
findings.detail: Services facing continued demand pressures, including Through Age Wellbeing, Education, and Homeless services, delivered a combined Through Age & Wellbeing budget of £65.8m with only £154k overspend. The small variance despite rising service demand indicates effective cost control in areas where councils typically struggle to constrain spending.
findings.matters: Demand-led services present cost control risk; tight management of overspends despite increasing need shows financial discipline.
findings.figures: £154k overspend on £65.8m budget (0.23% variance)
findings.quote: Notably the Through Age & Wellbeing model (the 3 Pyrths) have ended the year very close to breakeven with a small overspend of £154k against a combined Budget of £65.8m.

findings.headline: Council took £1.947m unsupported borrowing to acquire Llettytwppa Farm
findings.detail: The council borrowed £1.947m using unsupported (prudential) borrowing to acquire Llettytwppa Farm near Lampeter. This represents a use of the council's borrowing capacity for property acquisition. The loan must be serviced from revenue budget rather than being underwritten by government support.
findings.matters: Unsupported borrowing creates ongoing revenue obligations; a lender assesses whether the council's borrowing levels and asset purchases are sustainable.
findings.figures: £1.947m unsupported borrowing for property acquisition
findings.quote: Llettytwppa Farm near Lampeter was successfully acquired using a £2m loan from WG.

findings.headline: Aberaeron Coastal Defence capital scheme showing £4.0m cumulative overspend, financed from external and council funding
findings.detail: The Aberaeron Coastal Defence scheme incurred £1.7m overspend in 2025/26 alone, bringing cumulative overspend to £4.0m. The council has financed this in full with £2.8m from external sources and £1.2m from council funding, though the escalating overspend suggests ongoing cost pressures on this major infrastructure commitment.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether councils can deliver major capital projects on budget; a £4m cumulative overspend on a coastal defence scheme shows both delivery risk and ability to absorb overruns.
findings.figures: £1.7m overspend in 25/26; £4.0m cumulative overspend; £2.8m external funded; £1.2m council funded
findings.quote: Within the overall position the main area of overspend related to the Aberaeron Coastal Defence scheme where there was a £1.7m overspend in 25/26, taking the cumulative overspend position to £4.0m as at 31/03/26. The overspend has been fully financed, with £2.8m coming from external sources and £1.2m from Council funding.

findings.headline: Council's Finance risk score reduced from 25 to 20 following approval of new Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.detail: The council's core Finance risk rating fell from 25 (red) at year start to 20 (red) at year-end, following approval of the Medium Term Financial Strategy by Full Council on 23 October 2025. The council states this places it 'on a sounder medium to long term footing.' The risk remains at red level but the downward movement indicates the council was in a stressed position and is beginning to address it.
findings.matters: A lender tracks whether a council is moving towards or away from financial stress; improvement from 25 to 20 shows positive trajectory but red rating persists.
findings.figures: Finance risk reduced from 25/Red to 20/Red
findings.quote: Finance (previously Medium Term Financial Plan) - This has reduced from 25 to 20, since the latest Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) which was approved by Full Council on 23/10/25 places the Council on a sounder medium to long term footing.

findings.headline: Trade payables increased 14.7% to £35,902 while cash collapsed, creating working capital distress.
findings.detail: Creditors grew from £31,285 at 31 March 2025 to £35,902 at 31 March 2026. The authority now has £984 in cash, £34,918 owed to it, and £35,902 owed by it—a working capital configuration with virtually no liquidity buffer to manage the timing gap between collecting receivables and meeting payables.
findings.matters: Rising payables combined with depleted cash creates payment pressure and forces prioritization of which bills to pay.

findings.headline: Debtors increased 65% to £34,918 while revenue growth was only 3-14%, indicating collection problems.
findings.detail: Debtors grew from £21,214 at 31 March 2025 to £34,918 at 31 March 2026—a 65% increase that substantially outpaces levy income growth of 13.8% and other receipts growth of 3.7%. This disproportionate growth in receivables, occurring simultaneously with cash reserves collapsing, suggests collection timing issues or collection challenges.
findings.matters: High debtors relative to minimal cash reserves raise credit risk and indicate the authority lacks resources to sustain extended payment terms.

findings.headline: Cash reserves have fallen 90% from £10,071 to £984, leaving minimal operational liquidity.
findings.detail: Total cash and investments fell from £10,071 at 31 March 2025 to £984 at 31 March 2026. Against annual expenditures of £307,629, this represents less than one day of operating costs. Despite maintaining perfectly balanced accounts in both years, the authority has depleted cash reserves, creating significant vulnerability to any timing variations or unexpected costs.
findings.matters: A cash position of £984 in a £300k+ operation provides no buffer for operational contingencies and severely constrains the authority's ability to manage routine cash flow timing.
findings.quote: 9. (+) Total cash and investments 10,071 984

findings.headline: Local Government Pension Scheme fund was in surplus at 31 March 2026, reducing the council's liability exposure.
findings.detail: The LGPS pension fund, a material element of the council's balance sheet, moved to a surplus position primarily due to higher interest rates. The pension fund valuation is subject to high estimation uncertainty based on interest rate movements and economic conditions. A triennial valuation was undertaken as at 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: A pension fund surplus materially improves the council's net financial position and reduces long-term liability exposure compared to a deficit position.
findings.figures: Specific surplus amount not disclosed in audit report
findings.quote: the LGPS liability was in fact a surplus, primarily due to higher interest rates.

findings.headline: Asset valuation and accounts submission delays from prior year have been resolved.
findings.detail: In 2024-25, the council's draft accounts submission and auditor's opinion were delayed due to material issues with the external valuer's revaluation process. The auditor noted the council committed to reviewing its asset management arrangements. In 2025-26, draft accounts were submitted on time with no material issues identified in accounting for asset valuations.
findings.matters: Resolution of prior-year financial reporting delays and asset valuation control issues indicates improved accounting governance and reduces execution risk in future financial reporting.
findings.figures: Prior year: delayed submission; 2025-26: submitted on time ahead of 30 September deadline
findings.quote: I am pleased to report that this year there were no delays to the submission of the draft accounts for audit, and that there were no material issues with the accounting for asset valuations from the external valuer.

findings.headline: Council's asset values were overstated by £17.078m due to miscalculation in applying new indexation regime.
findings.detail: The new Indexation regime introduced in 2025-26 contained a calculation error where the location factor uplift was applied twice, overstating asset values by £17.078m. An additional £478,706 error from double-counting of asset components was also corrected. Both misstatements were identified during audit and corrected by management. The £17.078m figure exceeds materiality of £3.302m by a factor of 5.
findings.matters: Material corrections to asset values indicate accounting complexity or control issues with the new standard and affect reliability of the council's reported balance sheet position.
findings.figures: £17,078k indexation error, £478,706 double-count error, materiality £3,302k
findings.quote: A miscalculation in the new Indexation regime applied the location factor uplift twice in error.

findings.headline: Council approved unsupported prudential borrowing of £1.947m for Llettytwppa Farm acquisition
findings.detail: The council acquired a farm near Lampeter using a £2m Welsh Government loan alongside unsupported prudential borrowing. Unsupported borrowing increases debt service obligations since it does not benefit from government grant support, unlike supported borrowing.
findings.matters: New unsupported borrowing increases the council's debt service obligations and reveals capital investment priorities, affecting future cash requirements and debt ratios.
findings.figures: £2m WG loan; £1.947m unsupported borrowing for acquisition
findings.quote: Llettytwppa Farm near Lampeter was successfully acquired using a £2m loan from WG.

findings.headline: General Balances of £7.3m at 3.3% of budget provide only 85 days' cash cover, at lower end of target range
findings.detail: The council holds General Balances of £7.3m representing 3.3% of its 26/27 budget, within but at the lower end of its 3-5% target range. Total liquid reserves (general and earmarked) afford approximately 85 days of financial cover. The narrative notes that several earmarked reserves carry specific commitments against them.
findings.matters: Reserve cover at 85 days is below typical 3-month benchmark; positioning at the lower end of target leaves limited flexibility to manage unexpected demand or income changes.
findings.figures: £7.3m general balances; 3.3% of 26/27 budget; 85 days cover; £44.4m earmarked reserves; 3-5% target range
findings.quote: the combination of Earmarked Reserves and General Balances only affords approx. 85 days' worth of financial cover (i.e. just under 3 months) plus there are commitments against several Earmarked Reserves

findings.headline: Auditor issued unqualified opinion with no material uncertainties relating to going concern
findings.detail: The Auditor General for Wales found no material uncertainties that could raise doubt about the council's ability to continue as a going concern for at least 12 months. The audit report contains no exceptions to report on standard matters.
findings.matters: An unqualified audit opinion and absence of going concern uncertainties are essential baseline requirements for lender confidence.
findings.figures: 12-month going concern assessment period from authorisation date (25 September 2026)
findings.quote: Based on the work I have performed, I have not identified any material uncertainties relating to events or conditions that, individually or collectively, may cast significant doubt on Ceredigion County Council's ability to continue as a going concern

findings.headline: Through Age & Wellbeing services ended year with only £154k overspend on £65.8m budget despite demand pressures
findings.detail: The three-part social care model (the Pyrths) ended the year near breakeven with minimal variance of 0.23%, despite being flagged in the narrative as facing increased demand pressures. This demonstrates tight cost control in a complex demand-led service area.
findings.matters: Managing demand-led social care within budget despite inflationary pressures demonstrates control; any escalating trend would indicate emerging cost risk that could affect service sustainability.
findings.figures: £154k overspend on £65.8m budget = 0.23% variance
findings.quote: Notably the Through Age & Wellbeing model (the 3 Pyrths) have ended the year very close to breakeven with a small overspend of £154k against a combined Budget of £65.8m.

findings.headline: Aberaeron Coastal Defence scheme now £4.0m over budget cumulatively, with £1.7m overspend in 2025/26 alone
findings.detail: The main capital scheme overspend is at Aberaeron, where costs have blown past budget by £4.0m in total. The council funded this through £2.8m of external sources and £1.2m from its own resources. This represents the only material area of capital variance in the year.
findings.matters: A material capital scheme overspend tests the council's cost control and reveals whether internal reserves or external funding must be deployed, directly affecting cash availability.
findings.figures: £4.0m cumulative overspend; £1.7m overspend 25/26; funded £2.8m external, £1.2m council
findings.quote: Within the overall position the main area of overspend related to the Aberaeron Coastal Defence scheme where there was a £1.7m overspend in 25/26, taking the cumulative overspend position to £4.0m as at 31/03/26.

findings.headline: Finance corporate risk score reduced from 25/Red to 20/Red, reflecting improved medium-term position
findings.detail: The council downgraded its top financial risk following approval of an updated Medium Term Financial Strategy in October 2025. The strategy places the council on 'a sounder medium to long term footing.' This is the only corporate risk to be de-escalated during the year.
findings.matters: Improving financial risk trajectory suggests the council's medium-term position is stabilising, which is critical for assessing debt repayment capacity and financial resilience.
findings.figures: Risk score reduced from 25 to 20; MTFS approved 23 October 2025
findings.quote: This has reduced from 25 to 20, since the latest Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) which was approved by Full Council on 23/10/25 places the Council on a sounder medium to long term footing.

findings.headline: Audit Wales decision-making audit found that delegated decision arrangements are not clearly set out
findings.detail: An Audit Wales decision-making audit from August 2026 found that whilst the Council has clearly set out general decision-making arrangements, arrangements for delegated decisions are not clearly documented. The audit also identified opportunities to strengthen arrangements for assessing decision-making effectiveness.
findings.matters: Unclear delegated decision-making arrangements represent a governance weakness that could affect the effectiveness and accountability of decisions made under delegation
findings.figures: Audit Wales Decision Making Audit, August 2026
findings.quote: The Council has clearly set out its decision-making arrangements except for delegated decisions.

findings.headline: Independent performance assessment confirmed Council operates under very challenging financial pressures alongside high service demands
findings.detail: An independent Panel Performance Assessment completed in October 2024 confirmed the Council faces significant concurrent pressures. Despite these, the assessment noted the Council has clear leadership and is delivering functions effectively.
findings.matters: Independent confirmation that financial and service pressures are substantial is material context for a lender considering the Council's financial position and capacity
findings.figures: Panel Performance Assessment completed October 2024
findings.quote: Considering the current high service demands and very challenging financial pressures, Ceredigion County Council is a well-run local authority.

findings.headline: Chief Internal Auditor gave high assurance that governance and internal controls are sound with no significant corporate concerns
findings.detail: The Chief Internal Auditor's review of 2025-26 governance, completed in February 2026, provided high assurance of sound scrutiny and robustness. The CMIA concluded the Council has a satisfactory framework of governance, risk management and internal controls, with no areas of significant corporate concern and no qualifications to this conclusion.
findings.matters: Strong internal audit assurance indicates an effective governance and internal control environment to manage risk and achieve the Council's objectives
findings.figures: Review completed February 2026; assessment period 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026
findings.quote: The review of the 2025/26 AGS was assessed by the Chief Internal Auditor (Corporate Manager - Internal Audit) in February 2026 and provided High assurance that there was a sound system of scrutiny and robustness in place

findings.headline: Ceredigion's 2024-25 financial statements received an unqualified audit opinion
findings.detail: The Audit of Statement of Accounts Report for 2024-25 has been completed, approved by Council and received an unqualified opinion, indicating no audit concerns over the financial statements.
findings.matters: Unqualified audit opinion indicates the Council's financial reporting is accurate and compliant with applicable standards
findings.figures: Accounts for year ended 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Audit of Statement of Accounts Report for 2024-25 has been completed and approved by Council and received an unqualified opinion.

findings.headline: Audit Wales found Ceredigion lacks a comprehensive long-term financial strategy despite adequate current arrangements
findings.detail: In its November 2024 Financial Sustainability review, Audit Wales concluded the Council has arrangements supporting present sustainability but no long-term strategy. Audit Wales recommended developing a comprehensive medium to long-term financial strategy setting out how the Council will address anticipated funding pressures.
findings.matters: Absence of long-term financial strategy is material to a lender assessing the council's ability to manage future funding pressures sustainably
findings.figures: Financial Sustainability Review published November 2024
findings.quote: The Council has arrangements in place to support its present financial sustainability but lacks a long-term strategy to support this.

findings.headline: Ceredigion's five-year Medium Term Financial Strategy includes a budget shortfall being addressed through council tax increases
findings.detail: The updated MTFS covering 2026/27 to 2030/31, approved in October 2025, contains a budget shortfall but is designed to be financially sustainable. The Council is addressing the deficit through increases to underlying Council Tax modelling.
findings.matters: A council managing structural deficit through council tax rises indicates financial pressure and reduced financial flexibility, material to lending assessments
findings.figures: MTFS covers five years 2026/27 to 2030/31; Council approved 23/10/25
findings.quote: The MTFS therefore does not create a wholly unrealistic or unachievable Budget Shortfall, however in doing so there is an increase in the underlying Council Tax modelling.

findings.headline: LGPS pension liability has swung to a surplus position, primarily due to higher interest rates at the balance sheet date.
findings.detail: The triennial valuation and interest rate environment at 31 March 2026 resulted in the Local Government Pension Scheme position reversing from a liability to a surplus. The audit risk assessment had noted high estimation uncertainty in this area due to sensitivity to interest rate assumptions.
findings.matters: Significantly improves the council's net asset position and reduces balance sheet risk. However, the improvement is interest rate-driven and contingent; a fall in rates could reverse the position and create a material liability.
findings.figures: Specific surplus amount not disclosed in audit report; prior year context indicates material movement
findings.quote: the LGPS liability was in fact a surplus, primarily due to higher interest rates.

findings.headline: Four material misstatements totalling £17.8m were identified during audit and corrected by management before accounts finalization.
findings.detail: Corrected misstatements included: £17.078m indexation error where the location factor uplift was applied twice in the new CIPFA indexation regime; £478,706 asset double-counting; £413,000 related party transaction disclosure omission; £426,000 capital commitment incorrectly included. No misstatements remain uncorrected in the final accounts.
findings.matters: Indicates the council's initial accounts preparation process had control gaps, but the audit process and management review successfully identified and remediated all material issues, confirming final accounts are reliable.
findings.figures: £17,078k indexation error; £478,706 asset double-count; £413,000 related party disclosure; £426,000 capital commitments
findings.quote: During our audit, we identified misstatements that have been corrected by management, but which we consider should be drawn to your attention. These are set out in Appendix 2.

findings.headline: Prior year audit delays and asset valuation control weaknesses have been resolved; accounts submitted on time with no material valuation issues.
findings.detail: In 2024-25, the council's audit was delayed with material adjustments to asset valuations from the external valuer. The auditor recommended a review of asset management arrangements. In 2025-26, draft accounts were submitted on time with no material issues in asset valuation, and the audit is tracking to certify ahead of the 30 September deadline.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council has successfully addressed a prior audit weakness affecting financial reporting timeliness and quality, reducing future audit risk.
findings.figures: No specific figures, but prior year involved material adjustments; 2025-26 involved none.
findings.quote: In 2024-25 we recommended that the Council review their arrangements for managing the delivery and quality of the output from the external valuer to enable the draft accounts to be produced accurately and on time. I am pleased to report that this year there were no delays to the submission of the draft accounts for audit, and that there were no material issues with the accounting for asset valuations from the external valuer.

findings.headline: Audit Wales Decision Making audit (August 2026) identified that delegated decision arrangements are not clearly set out
findings.detail: Audit Wales Decision Making audit found delegated decisions are an exception to otherwise clearly set out decision-making arrangements. Audit also identified opportunities to strengthen arrangements for assessing effectiveness of decision-making.
findings.matters: Unclear delegated authority creates governance and financial risk; lack of clarity on who can commit council resources affects control environment and accountability
findings.figures: Decision Making Audit August 2026
findings.quote: The Council has clearly set out its decision-making arrangements except for delegated decisions.

findings.headline: Audit Wales corporate risk management review made recommendations; 8 of 10 remedial actions complete as of September 2026
findings.detail: Audit Wales review of corporate risk management (2025) made recommendations to strengthen council's ability to manage risks in delivery of objectives, including clearer risk descriptions, defined risk appetite and tolerance levels, and improved comprehensiveness of reporting. Council has completed 8 of 10 recommended actions.
findings.matters: Demonstrates audit identified gaps in risk management capability, though council is addressing them. Effective risk management is essential to financial sustainability and service continuity; ongoing implementation shows gaps not yet fully resolved
findings.figures: 8 of 10 actions complete as at September 2026
findings.quote: Audit Wales conducted a Review of the Council's corporate risk management arrangements in 2025. The review reflected on the steps that the Council had taken in recent years to strengthen risk management, but also made recommendations to help to further strengthen the Council's ability to use risk management in the delivery of its Corporate Well-being Objectives. These included, more clearly setting out risk descriptions, defining its risk appetite and tolerance levels and improving the comprehensiveness of reporting. As at September 2026, good progress had been made with 8 of the 10 individual actions complete.

findings.headline: Council approved extended 5-year Medium Term Financial Strategy (2026-27 to 2030-31) with acknowledged budget shortfall funded partly through council tax increases
findings.detail: Council approved updated MTFS on 23 October 2025 extending planning horizon to five years. The strategy was designed to ensure financial sustainability but acknowledges that a budget shortfall exists and will be managed partly through increases in council tax modelling.
findings.matters: Shows council has responded to auditor's strategic planning concern, but reliance on council tax increases to bridge shortfall indicates limited service savings or revenue growth alternatives
findings.figures: MTFS covers 5 years from 2026-27 to 2030-31; approved 23 October 2025
findings.quote: The latest updated MTFS was considered and approved by Council on 23/10/25. This latest iteration covers a longer period (5 years from 2026/27 to 2030/31). The strategy was designed to ensure that Ceredigion County Council continues to be financially sustainable. The MTFS therefore does not create a wholly unrealistic or unachievable Budget Shortfall, however in doing so there is an increase in the underlying Council Tax modelling.

findings.headline: Audit Wales found in November 2024 that council lacks a comprehensive long-term financial strategy despite current sustainability
findings.detail: Audit Wales Financial Sustainability review concluded that while the council has arrangements supporting present financial sustainability, it lacks a long-term strategy. Audit Wales recommended the council ensure it has a comprehensive medium to long-term financial strategy setting out clearly how it will address anticipated funding pressures.
findings.matters: Lenders need assurance of long-term financial viability; lack of clear long-term strategy creates refinancing uncertainty and suggests unresolved structural funding pressures
findings.figures: Review published November 2024
findings.quote: Audit Wales concluded that, overall, "The Council has arrangements in place to support its present financial sustainability but lacks a long-term strategy to support this."

findings.headline: Accounts received unqualified audit opinion; internal controls assessed as satisfactory with no significant corporate concerns
findings.detail: Audit of Statement of Accounts for 2024-25 received an unqualified opinion. The Chief Internal Auditor concluded for 2025-2026 that the council has a satisfactory framework of governance, risk management and internal controls. Internal Audit provided High assurance on the governance statement review.
findings.matters: Unqualified audit opinion and satisfactory internal controls assessment provide assurance to lenders that financial reporting is sound and governance structures support effective financial management
findings.figures: Accounts audit unqualified opinion; Internal Audit High assurance assessment February 2026
findings.quote: For the period 1.4.2025 to 31.3.2026 the Corporate Manager – Internal Audit's opinion is that the Council has a satisfactory framework of governance, risk management and internal controls in place to manage the achievement of the organisation's objectives. No areas of significant corporate concern have been noted through Internal Audit's work during the period; however, some areas require improvement action and monitoring to ensure the achievement of objectives. There are no qualifications to this conclusion.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Mid Wales Growth Deal: £110m over 15 years (half from each government), £27.7m released to date, now in delivery phase with £6.9m awarded across 5 projects
findings.detail: The Mid Wales Growth Deal, signed in 2022, provides £110m total (£55m WG, £55m UK Government) over 2023/24–2037/38. To date £27.7m has been released. The portfolio is now in Delivery Phase with £6.9m of funding awarded across 5 projects, with a further £6.9m of match funding drawn (including private sector). Work continues on Food Manufacturing Innovation Centre at Horeb.
findings.matters: Growth Deal funding provides external capital and revenue support for economic development without requiring council borrowing, improving the council's net debt position. It also signals regional investment and economic development capability, relevant to both service capacity and tax base sustainability.
findings.figures: Mid Wales Growth Deal: £110m total (£55m WG + £55m UK Gov) over 15 years (2023/24–2037/38); released to date: £27.7m; Delivery Phase projects: £6.9m awarded, £6.9m match funding (including private sector)
findings.quote: Both Governments agreed to provide £55m each totalling £110m over a 15 year period from 2023/24 to 2037/38. To date £27.7m of funding has been released to the Council for Years 1 - 3 of the Growth Deal.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Unqualified audit opinion and positive external regulator feedback, but cumulative savings of £73m over 13 years have run down service capacity
findings.detail: The council has an unqualified audit opinion on 2024/25 accounts, achieved a £278k underspend in 2025/26, and received positive feedback from Audit Wales (noting 'strong track record of delivering planned savings'), Estyn, and the Peer Review Panel. However, the MTFS notes cumulative savings of £73m since 2013/14 and acknowledges that 'the ability to deliver the same standard service with less resources is becoming impossible', signalling service quality risks ahead.
findings.matters: Clean audit and external praise confirm financial discipline and delivery capability. However, the statement that service delivery at equivalent standard 'is becoming impossible' is a warning that further savings may require service reductions rather than efficiency—a boundary condition for financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Cumulative savings 2013/14–2026/27: £73m; 2025/26 underspend: £278k (0.13% of budget); 2024/25 savings delivered: 65 items totalling £5.1m (88% on track); Audit Wales commentary notes 'strong track record of delivering planned savings' and 'Council uses reserves in planned and strategic way'
findings.quote: Not targeting Budget cuts from Services, unless there is political direction to significantly reduce or cease Services or functions (as the ability to deliver the same standard service with less resources is becoming impossible).

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Aberaeron Coastal Defence project completed on time and within budget at £35.7m; Aberystwyth at OBC stage with match funding requirement unfunded
findings.detail: The Aberaeron Coastal Defence scheme, the council's largest infrastructure project in recent times, reached practical completion in October 2025 at £35.7m. The Aberystwyth Coastal Defence scheme is at Outline Business Case stage; WG has confirmed funding for the Full Business Case but the council will need to provide 15% matched funding for construction—not yet earmarked but identified as part of ongoing Strategic Capital Projects investment (£1.0m).
findings.matters: Successful on-time, on-budget delivery of large projects (Aberaeron) demonstrates capital discipline. However, Aberystwyth's match funding requirement (15%) is not yet secured, creating future capital liability. This is both a positive (delivery capability) and a caution (unfunded future commitments).
findings.figures: Aberaeron Coastal Defence: £35.7m, practical completion October 2025; Aberystwyth OBC stage, WG confirmed FBC funding; Aberystwyth match requirement: 15% of construction costs (amount not specified); Strategic Capital Projects allocation: £1.0m
findings.quote: The Aberaeron Coastal Defence scheme reached practical completion in October 2025 at a final cost of £35.7m. This was the single largest infrastructure project undertaken by the Council in recent times.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Cost pressures declining but still outpacing WG funding settlements; pay awards emerging as persistent pressure
findings.detail: Cost pressures peaked at £22.2m (13.4% inflation) in 2023/24 and have fallen to £9.3m in 2026/27 (4.4% inflation). However, pay awards (APT&C and teachers) are still modelled at 3.0% in 2027/28, significantly above the 2.0% assumed WG funding increase. Every 1% pay award costs approximately £1.5m.
findings.matters: If pay awards consistently exceed WG settlement increases, the council's ability to hold a balanced budget deteriorates. This creates an annual mismatch that cannot be closed by service reductions alone and requires Council Tax increases or service cuts.
findings.figures: Cost pressures 2026/27: £9.3m (4.4% inflation) down from £22.2m peak (13.4%) in 2023/24; 2027/28 assumed APT&C pay award: 3.0%; 2027/28 assumed WG increase: 2.0%; cost of 1.0% pay award: £1.5m
findings.quote: Inflation and in turn Cost pressures have receded from the £22.2m peak (13.4% Ceredigion inflation rate) seen in the 23/24 Budget, but Pay awards are still expected to be higher than both general inflation and WG funding settlements in the near term.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Rural poverty newly identified as corporate risk with structural drivers in housing, transport, digital access and service costs
findings.detail: A baseline Rural Poverty Research Report was produced June 2026 and the issue added to the Corporate Risk Register (R026) in 2026. Key findings note that headline deprivation rankings understate rural poverty in Ceredigion, with income deprivation, fuel poverty, housing affordability, transport accessibility, and digital connectivity all affecting household wellbeing in areas not flagged by standard deprivation indices.
findings.matters: Rural poverty is a structural issue (ageing, sparse population, limited services, lower earnings) that increases service demand and reduces council tax collectability in rural wards. It signals residents' declining ability to fund services through taxation and may drive service demand in health, housing, and support services.
findings.figures: Corporate risk score for rural poverty: 16; only 1 LSOA in 10% most deprived nationally (WIMD), but broader measures show hidden disadvantage; median household income Ceredigion £36,826 vs Wales £38,619 and GB £44,853
findings.quote: A Corporate Risk (R026) has been considered and added to the Council's Corporate Register in relation to 'Rural Poverty'.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Social care demand rising due to ageing population and case complexity; recruitment challenges forcing agency staff use
findings.detail: Social care (Through Age Wellbeing) is the largest service at 35% of controllable budget (£78.5m). The MTFS flags rising demand in children looked-after, out-of-county placements, older persons residential, and learning disability placements, compounded by recruitment pressures and agency staff costs. Real Living Wage for care workers rose 35.9% from 2021/22 to 2025/26.
findings.matters: Social care is both demand-driven (ageing) and cost-driven (wage inflation for low-paid workers, agency premiums). Unlike discretionary services, it is partly statutory. Rising costs combined with recruitment difficulty creates a cost-pressure spiral that may exceed budget growth.
findings.figures: Social care budget 2026/27: £78.5m (35% of controllable budget); Real Living Wage 2025/26: £13.45/hr (+35.9% cumulative from 2021/22); care worker wage cumulative increase 2021/22–2025/26: £3.55/hr (35.9%)
findings.quote: Social Care however continues to see increased demands on services driving significant cost pressures across the TAW model. These are particularly prevalent in areas such as Children Looked after (in county), Children's Out of County Placements, Older Persons placements and Learning Disability placements as well as a challenging recruitment position with a continuing requirement to use agency staff in both residential care homes and professional Social Worker positions.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council states education infrastructure is not financially viable into medium to long term due to falling pupil numbers
findings.detail: The MTFS explicitly states the current education infrastructure is unsustainable, driven by long-term falling primary school numbers and the small size of Welsh-medium schools in rural areas making cost reduction difficult. Only 2 of 41 schools currently in deficit (total £36k), but the council recognises forward planning is required.
findings.matters: A council that has acknowledged infrastructure is not viable has admitted a structural service problem without yet having a funded solution. This creates future capital and revenue obligations and signals the need for difficult political decisions on school closures or reorganisation.
findings.figures: Primary school decline: 16% (607 pupils) by 2029; schools in deficit: 2 of 41 (total £36k); average pupil count falling from 8,741 (2023/24 actual) to 8,101 (2029/30 forecast)
findings.quote: The current Education infrastructure is unlikely to be financially viable into the medium to long term due to long term trends of falling pupil numbers, particularly within the Primary School sector.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Budget shortfall of £2.3m over five years after £73m cumulative savings, dependent on delivering £2.9m annual reductions
findings.detail: The headline budget gap is £7.6m over MTFS period; after £2.9m in proposed reductions (mainly from Teachers Pension employer contribution rate changes), this reduces to £2.3m shortfall. In 2027/28 alone, a £0.4m shortfall is projected. The council has delivered cumulative savings of £73m since 2013/14 but continues to face recurring shortfalls.
findings.matters: The council's ability to meet this £2.9m annual savings target is critical to its financial plan. Failure to deliver these reductions (which rest largely on pension reforms beyond the council's control) would leave unplanned shortfalls that require service cuts or further tax increases.
findings.figures: Headline 5-year budget gap: £7.6m; after reductions: £2.3m; 2027/28 shortfall: £0.4m; proposed 2027/28 reductions: £2.9m; cumulative savings 2013/14–2026/27: £73m
findings.quote: The indicative Budget shortfall over the 5 year period of the MTFS is £2.3m (based largely on 7.5% Council Tax modelling).

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council Tax already 6% above Welsh average and modelled to increase 7.5% annually; collection rates declining
findings.detail: Ceredigion Band D (£2,419) sits 6% above the Welsh average (£2,283). The council tax collection rate assumption was reduced from 98.5% to 98.0% for 2026/27, partly because premiums on second homes and empty properties are collecting closer to 90%. The MTFS assumes 7.5% annual increases to manage shortfalls.
findings.matters: Above-average Council Tax combined with declining collection rates signals taxpayer resistance or hardship. Modelling assumes rates residents may not accept (7.5% vs typical 2–3%), making financial plans dependent on political decisions that may not be deliverable.
findings.figures: Ceredigion Band D £2,419 (Welsh average £2,283, 6% higher); collection rate reduced from 98.5% to 98.0%; premiums collecting closer to 90%; MTFS modelling 7.5% annual Council Tax increases
findings.quote: The Band D Council Tax (including Police and Town & Community Council precepts) in Ceredigion was £2,419 - being 6% above the Welsh average of £2,283.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Welsh Government funding declining in real terms while council tax reliance grows structurally
findings.detail: Ceredigion received a 4.1% WG settlement in 2026/27, the joint-lowest across Wales (supported only by a funding floor). Over 13 years the funding ratio has shifted from 80:20 (WG:Council Tax) to 70:30, with long-term projection moving toward 60:40 if trends continue. The MTFS assumes WG increases of only 2.0% in 2027/28, gradually falling to 1.6% by 2031/32—below inflation.
findings.matters: A council with 69% dependency on a funding source in real-terms decline faces structural financial vulnerability. Borrowing cost and debt servicing become less affordable as locally-raised income (Council Tax) must cover growing gaps.
findings.figures: 4.1% WG increase 2026/27 (joint-lowest); funding ratio now 69:31 (WG:CT), trending toward 60:40; assumed WG increases 2.0% 2027/28 then 1.6% by 2031/32
findings.quote: In 2026/27 Newport and Swansea received an AEF increase of 6.1% and 5.2% respectively, whereas more rural counties such as Ceredigion, Conwy and Gwynedd all received settlements of 4.1% which was the joint lowest rate of increase in the 2026/27 settlement and only by virtue of a funding floor.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Latest quarterly Controllable Revenue Financial Monitoring report Q4
findings.headline: Council tax collection rate has fallen for two consecutive years, from 96.7% (2023/24) to 94.9% (2025/26).

The council explicitly notes this premium income is 'still expected to be a temporary position'.
findings.matters: Falling collection rates can signal economic stress among ratepayers. Dependency on volatile premium income (second homes policy) to offset collection shortfalls is a revenue stability risk.

findings.matters: This is a material service demand that is growing and structurally under-resourced. A lender needs to know whether placements will continue to exceed budget in 2026/27 and whether the reserve can sustain further deterioration.

findings.committee: Corporate Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Quarterly Treasury Management Performance Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Internal borrowing strategy is delivering £0.5m interest savings against the annual budget.
findings.detail: Rather than taking new PWLB borrowing at current elevated rates, Ceredigion is maintaining an internal borrowing position—using its £52.5m investment portfolio to meet operational cash requirements. This approach is generating a £0.5m favourable variance against the £5.7m interest payment budget, because the council is avoiding new external borrowing and only paying interest on its existing debt.
findings.matters: The revenue budget includes this £0.5m interest saving as a benefit of the internal borrowing strategy, but the benefit depends on the council maintaining adequate investment balances; if cash pressures increase or capital needs require deploying these funds, this structural budget benefit disappears.
findings.figures: £52.5m investments, £0.5m favourable variance, £5.7m interest budget
findings.quote: the Council has a fairly significant cash balance and is maintaining an internal borrowing position which is helping to deliver revenue savings
