findings.paper_title: Appendix 2- Latest quarterly Capital Financial Monitoring report Q1 26-27
findings.headline: Museum roof project overrun exhausts contingency with £350k shortfall and no confirmed funding solution
findings.detail: The Ceredigion Museum roof project hit unforeseen building condition issues when demolition revealed historic water ingress and structural work needed on stonework, steelwork and timber elements. The contingency sum held for the project has already been exhausted. The scheme cost has risen from £1.350m to an estimated £1.700m, leaving a £350k gap that the council is exploring external grant funding to cover.
findings.matters: A 26% cost overrun on a heritage project with contingency already spent signals project management issues and ties up capital resources that may need to come from elsewhere; a lender assessing the council's ability to deliver capital programmes would note the need to find additional external funding mid-project.
findings.figures: Original budget £1.350m, latest estimated cost £1.700m, shortfall £350k
findings.quote: additional costs have been encountered due to unforeseen building condition issues that were uncovered when the old roof was being removed. The building is Grade 2 listed and is over 100 years old, so although a contingency sum was held for the project this has already been exhausted.

findings.paper_title: c) Report- Quarterly Treasury Management Performance Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Council deferring £4.6m planned PWLB borrowing due to elevated rates, waiting for optimum rate
findings.detail: Council expects to borrow £4.6m from PWLB for highways maintenance (funded by Welsh Government), but is delaying while rates remain elevated following Middle East conflict. Strong investment balances provide flexibility to defer until rates improve.
findings.matters: Shows rate sensitivity and financial flexibility, but also means planned highways capital spending timing depends on borrowing decisions
findings.figures: £4.6m planned PWLB borrowing; PWLB rates elevated; significant investment balances allow deferral
findings.quote: The Council is monitoring PWLB borrowing rates with the aim of securing an optimum rate. However, as noted above, it is able to delay this borrowing if necessary while rates remain relatively high.

findings.paper_title: c) Report- Quarterly Treasury Management Performance Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Net debt improved by £12.1m in Q1 to £74.4m, driven by higher investment holdings
findings.detail: External debt remained stable at £126.9m, but investment holdings rose from £40.4m to £52.5m, improving net debt from £86.5m to £74.4m. The council is maintaining an internal borrowing position to generate this benefit.
findings.matters: Improving net debt and strengthening cash position indicates improved financial headroom and flexibility
findings.figures: Net Debt £86.5m (31 March 2026) to £74.4m (30 June 2026); Investments £40.4m to £52.5m
findings.quote: The Council's summarised debt and investment position is shown below, with further details analysed in Appendix A (Investments) and Appendix B (Debt). Net Debt 86.5  74.4

findings.paper_title: a) Report- 26-27 Controllable Revenue Budget - Q1
findings.headline: Aberystwyth promenade parking scheme underperforming: £100k shortfall against £500k budget, with winter uncertainty
findings.detail: Parking charges began 18 May 2026. By 26 July (70 days), the scheme generated £90.6k (£1,294/day average, rising to £1,555 since 01/07). Forecast is now £400k against the £500k budget—a £100k shortfall. The council flags uncertainty over winter months as a key risk, and note that 7 weeks of the year had no charging possible.
findings.matters: A new revenue stream intended to be material (£500k) is underperforming by 20%. If this is structural, it adds to income pressure. The seasonal pattern suggests further deterioration in winter is plausible.
findings.figures: £90,614 over 70 days, £1,294/day average, forecast £400k vs £500k budget (£100k shortfall)
findings.quote: At this early stage in the year, income forecasts are for c£400k of income for the 26/27 financial year (against a Budget of £500k). Note that no charging was possible for just under 7 weeks at the start of the year and it remains to be seen how space occupancy will fare during the winter months.

findings.paper_title: a) Report- 26-27 Controllable Revenue Budget - Q1
findings.headline: Welsh Government's 1st Supplementary Budget did not pass, leaving £40-47m in potential school and childcare funding at risk
findings.detail: WG's proposed supplementary budget included £40m capital for school maintenance, £15m for free secondary school meals, £2m for school swimming, £10m childcare capital, and £47m childcare revenue support. With the budget failing, it is unclear whether these commitments will be delivered later in the year or abandoned. WG policy changes (TA level transitions, ALN coordinator pay scales, expanded maternity pay) also lack full funding clarity.
findings.matters: Service and budget planning is dependent on funding that has not been confirmed. If WG fails to find alternative funding for school meals, swimming, or childcare, Ceredigion may face unbudgeted service delivery gaps or pressure to cut. The ALN system is noted as experiencing 'unprecedented levels of demand, complexity and cost' with no additional funding committed.
findings.figures: £40m capital school maintenance, £15m free school meals, £2m school swimming, £10m childcare capital, £47m childcare revenue
findings.quote: With the 1st Supplementary Budget not passing, it remains to be seen how / if these elements will still impact on Local Government later in the financial year.

findings.paper_title: a) Report- 26-27 Controllable Revenue Budget - Q1
findings.headline: Reserve cover of only 85 days (less than 3 months) against £221.5m budget, with commitments already assigned
findings.detail: Combined General Balances (£7.3m) and Earmarked Reserves (£44.4m) total £51.7m, providing only 85 days of financial cover. Multiple commitments already assigned: match-funding for capital schemes, Digital Strategy delivery, Corporate Wellbeing Objectives. The council is already drawing reserves for placements and agency staffing this year.
findings.matters: Thin reserves leave no buffer for service shocks or revenue shortfalls. A lender should note the council lacks financial resilience; the 85-day cover is below prudent levels, and reserves are being deployed to mask structural budget pressures.
findings.figures: £51.7m total reserves, £221.5m budget, 85 days cover, £44.4m earmarked (already committed)
findings.quote: However, relative to the Council's £221.5m budget, the combination of Earmarked Reserves and General Balances still only affords approximately 85 days' worth of financial cover (less than 3 months). There are also commitments against several Earmarked Reserves (e.g. matched funding for major capital schemes, delivery of the Digital Strategy and funding to support the delivery of the 4 Corporate Wellbeing Objectives).

findings.paper_title: a) Report- 26-27 Controllable Revenue Budget - Q1
findings.headline: Pay award settlements significantly higher than budgeted 2.75% assumption, with NJC award still rejected by all unions
findings.detail: The 26/27 budget assumed 2.75% pay awards. NJC offered 3.3% in March but all 3 unions rejected it and outcome remains unresolved. Teachers are receiving 3.5-5.0% (effective 01/09/26, with WG to fund the increase), Soulbury staff 3.6%. Chief Officers accepted 3.3%. The council notes this creates risk of needing to review priorities if awards exceed budget.
findings.matters: Pay awards are a major cost driver and uncertainty. If NJC settles significantly higher than 2.75%, the £230k overspend becomes structural and reserves will be needed to absorb it. The council's own assessment flags this as a risk.
findings.figures: Budget assumed 2.75%, NJC rejected 3.3%, Teachers 3.5-5.0%, Soulbury 3.6%, Chief Officers 3.3%
findings.quote: The main pay awards are yet to reach formal determination stage. For NJC general staff, in late March 2026 the National Employers offered a 3.3% pay award with effect from 01/04/26 but this has been rejected by all 3 Unions.

findings.paper_title: a) Report- 26-27 Controllable Revenue Budget - Q1
findings.headline: Council tax in-year collection rate falling: down 0.6% to 35.6%, with collections on second homes particularly weak at 87.3%
findings.detail: The in-year collection rate has fallen from 36.2% (25/26) to 35.6% in Q1 26/27. A permanent 1% fall equals £780k annually. Collections on second homes are especially weak (87.3%, down from 91.6%) despite higher premiums intended to drive properties back into use. Properties with premiums show cumulative collection rates of only 69.2% for accounts with both premiums, suggesting enforcement challenges.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates threaten revenue stability. The council is relying on premium income gains and reserve drawdown to offset collection weakness, which is not a sustainable strategy for a lender's counterparty.
findings.figures: In-year collection rate 35.6% (down from 36.2%), second homes collection 87.3% (down from 91.6%), 1% permanent fall = £780k impact
findings.quote: The in-year Council Tax collection rate position continues to fall relative to the previous year and at the early stage in the year is c0.6% lower than 25/26.

findings.paper_title: a) Report- 26-27 Controllable Revenue Budget - Q1
findings.headline: Agency staffing costs in social care total £1.9m+ across two services, with £500k masked by reserve draw
findings.detail: Porth Cynnal projects £1.165m net cost for agency staff (reduced to £665k by drawing £500k from reserves). Porth Gofal forecasts £782k net agency overspend. Despite council terms being 'relatively attractive', recruitment challenges in frontline Social Worker and care roles persist. The council is managing the position through reserves rather than addressing the structural cost.
findings.matters: A lender should identify whether high agency costs reflect temporary vacancy drag or structural recruitment failure. Here, the £500k reserve transfer masks the true run-rate cost; if sustained, this is £2m+ of structural pressure.
findings.figures: £1.165m Porth Cynnal agency cost, £782k Porth Gofal agency cost, £500k reserve assumed draw
findings.quote: Despite the Council's terms and conditions being relatively attractive, recruitment challenges remain with a net cost of £1.165m being projected within Porth Cynnal for agency staff covering frontline Social Worker roles (£500k has been assumed from reserves to bring this total down to £665k).

findings.paper_title: a) Report- 26-27 Controllable Revenue Budget - Q1
findings.headline: Out-of-county children's placements forecast to overspend by £1.7m, requiring additional reserve drawdown
findings.detail: Q1 has been challenging for Children Looked After with 24 residential and 9 college placements forecast at £9.7m gross cost. The council will transfer £1.7m from the Placement Equalization reserve in 26/27, on top of a budgeted £840k transfer already planned. A third in-county facility received CIW approval in July which should help, but current placement costs remain a structural problem.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if services are being delivered by drawing down finite reserves rather than sustainable budget. Placement costs are growing and eroding the council's financial cushion.
findings.figures: £9.7m forecast gross cost, £1.739m overspend, £1.7m additional reserve transfer required, £2.1m in-county facility budget
findings.quote: Total Gross expenditure on out of county placements for 26/27 is forecast at £9.7m resulting in a forecast overspend of £1.739m which will be transferred from the Placement Equalisation reserve (on top of a budgeted transfer of £840k).

findings.paper_title: b) Report- Q1 Capital Programme Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Ceredigion Museum roof project has overrun by £350k due to structural defects discovered during works, with contingency exhausted.
findings.detail: The original budget for the museum roof was £1.350m. When removal of the old roof began, unforeseen building condition issues were uncovered, including historic water ingress in walls and damaged stonework, steelwork and timber lintels requiring rectification. The estimated total scheme cost is now £1.700m. Although a contingency was held, it has been exhausted, and the council is now exploring external grant funding to cover the shortfall.
findings.matters: A 26% cost overrun on a capital project signals deficient project controls and cost estimation, and means the council will need to secure additional funding, potentially requiring external borrowing or grant applications.
findings.figures: Original budget £1.350m, revised estimated cost £1.700m, shortfall £350k
findings.quote: The latest estimated total scheme cost is £1.700m versus an original budget of £1.350m. Funding options for the estimated shortfall are currently being explored including exploring external grant funding.

findings.headline: Investment income declined below budget, council transferred reserves specifically to address falling returns
findings.detail: Investment income fell £39k short of budget at £1.405m actual versus £1.444m budgeted. The council explicitly transferred £256k to reserves to build resilience against declining investment income, suggesting this is an expected ongoing concern rather than a one-off variance.
findings.matters: Declining investment returns reduce the council's internally-generated cash income and signal expected continued pressure on investment yields.
findings.figures: £1.405m actual against £1.444m budget, £256k reserve transfer earmarked for declining investment income
findings.quote: This position has enabled a transfer to reserves (£212k) to provide additional resilience as a result of the elevated level of financial risk in relation to the impact of the Middle East conflict and additional resilience (£256k) against declining Investment Income.

findings.headline: PWLB borrowing rates elevated to upper range following Middle East conflict escalation
findings.detail: Long-term PWLB rates rose to the upper end of their range following the conflict escalation in March 2026 and have remained there. The 49½-50 year rate stands at 6.40% and the 24½-25 year rate at 6.60%, significantly higher than where they began the year.
findings.matters: Any future capital borrowing by the council will face these elevated rates, materially increasing the cost of borrowing and affecting capital investment decisions.
findings.figures: 49½-50 year PWLB rate 6.40%, 24½-25 year PWLB rate 6.60%
findings.quote: Since the escalation of the conflict in the middle east in March 2026, rates have risen to the upper end of that range, where they have remained.

findings.headline: Highways Infrastructure Renewal scheme required additional revenue funding to cover £160k overspend
findings.detail: The Highways Infrastructure Renewal and Improvements scheme was budgeted at £2.080m but actual expenditure was £2.240m. The council covered the £160k shortfall by using additional revenue funding rather than containing the overspend within the capital allocation.
findings.matters: Raid­ing revenue budgets to cover capital overspends reduces financial flexibility elsewhere and suggests poor cost control on ongoing programmes.
findings.figures: Budgeted £2.080m, actual £2.240m, overspend £160k funded from additional revenue contribution.
findings.quote: Highways Infrastructure Renewal / Improvements * (160)... * Funded via an additional revenue contribution

findings.headline: Aberaeron Coastal Protection Scheme completed £4m over its original £31.6m budget
findings.detail: This major capital scheme achieved practical completion on 30 September 2025 and is now in a 12-month defects liability period. The original scheme budget was £31.590m but actual expenditure reached £35.597m. Funding included Welsh Government supported borrowing of £24.907m, council reserves and general funding of £4.739m, and additional external funding including £1m from UK Shared Prosperity funding.
findings.matters: A 12.7% overspend on a major scheme signals cost control and project delivery weaknesses. For a lender, this raises questions about the council's ability to manage large capital programmes and whether reserves will be adequate for future schemes.
findings.figures: Original budget £31.590m, actual expenditure £35.597m, overspend approximately £4.0m. Contractor costs: BAM Nuttall £33.937m, Atkins £1.387m, internal capital salaries £217k.
findings.quote: From a pure financial perspective the scheme did incur additional costs, in line with the position previously reported – i.e. Costs exceeded the Project Budget by c£4.0m.

findings.headline: External audit and legal fees overran budget, signalling cost pressures from external suppliers.
findings.detail: Legal & Governance Services overspent by £50k, driven by 'increased court, legal and external audit fees.' The Audit Services line specifically notes 'higher than budgeted external audit fees.' This is a cost the council cannot easily control and suggests external service inflation.
findings.matters: Uncontrollable cost pressures from external auditors and legal services are a warning sign of sector-wide cost inflation. This is hard to budget for and will recur.
findings.figures: Legal & Governance overspend £50k; Audit Services overspend £24k; overall service overspend primarily due to increased fees
findings.quote: Overall the Service has overspent slightly, mainly as a result of increased court, legal and external audit fees.

findings.headline: Middle East conflict creating emerging financial risk: £1.0m Cost & Inflationary Pressures reserve now held, with fuel and mileage rate impacts anticipated.
findings.detail: The council has increased the Cost & Inflationary Pressures reserve to £1.0m following the Middle East conflict. The paper notes: 'The path for interest rates has changed as a result of the Middle East conflict, with inflation expected to rise in the short term.' Anticipated uses include increased fuel costs for the vehicle fleet and elevated HMRC mileage rates. Impact on 25/26 was limited due to timing, but the council is flagging this as an emerging risk.
findings.matters: Inflation in fuel and transport costs can spread quickly through council budgets. The council is signalling real uncertainty about cost inflation ahead.
findings.figures: £212k transferred to Cost & Inflationary Pressures reserve; reserve now £1.0m
findings.quote: The £212k transferred to the Cost & Inflationary Pressures reserve means £1.0m is now held in that reserve to assist with mitigation where needed. Anticipated uses at this stage include the increased cost of fuel for the Council's Vehicle fleet and the impact of the increased HMRC mileage rate.

findings.headline: General Balances stand at 3.3% of budget, at the bottom of the council's own 3–5% target range with limited headroom.
findings.detail: General Balances of £7.3m represent 3.3% of the 2026/27 budget, sitting at the lower end of the council's stated target range of 3–5%. Combined with £44.4m in earmarked reserves (many with specific commitments), total liquid cover is only approximately 85 days. The Section 151 officer's opinion of 'low risk of a Section 114 notice' is explicitly conditional on the council continuing to pass a balanced budget each year.
findings.matters: Minimal reserves headroom leaves little cushion for overspends, emergency spend, or income shocks. The Section 114 assessment is conditional, not an unconditional all-clear.
findings.figures: General Balances £7.3m (3.3% of 2026/27 budget of £221m); Earmarked Reserves £44.4m; Combined cover ~85 days
findings.quote: The Council's General Balances ending the year at £7.3m, equating to 3. 3% of the Council's 2026/27 Budget. This is an important metric as the Council aims to keep within a target range of 3% and 5%... the combination of Earmarked Reserves and General Balances only affords approx. 85 days' worth of financial cover (i.e. just under 3 months)

findings.headline: Council tax collection rate has declined for two consecutive years, falling to 94.9% from 96.7%.
findings.detail: Collection rates fell from 96.7% in 23/24 to 95.5% in 24/25 to 94.9% in 25/26. The paper notes 'the rate of decline has slowed' and that higher second homes premium collections offset the decline this year, but the underlying trend is negative. The paper also states the position 'is still expected to be a temporary position with further behavioural change expected', suggesting uncertainty about reversibility.
findings.matters: A two-year collection rate decline signals difficulty in recovering debt or a shift in the council's tax base. The council's assumption that this is temporary and reversible is not assured.
findings.quote: The in-year Council Tax collection rate position has fallen for the second consecutive year, however the rate of decline has slowed in 25/26.

findings.headline: Adult social care agency costs reached £352k net overspend in Porth Gofal alone, with recruitment challenges unresolved.
findings.detail: Porth Gofal (older persons and disability services, £19.6m budget) recorded a £85k overspend driven by £352k in net agency staff costs. The paper states: 'Social care continues to face recruitment challenges, despite the Council's terms and conditions being relatively attractive.' Porth Cynnal (learning disabilities and mental health, £41.2m budget) also overspent by £390k despite 'relatively attractive' terms. Both services remain volatile with pressures at the 'front door'.
findings.matters: Agency staffing costs in social care are typically unsustainable and hard to control. If recruitment remains difficult and terms are already attractive, wage pressure is likely, and there is little room to reduce costs.
findings.figures: Porth Gofal: £352k net agency overspend; £85k total service overspend on £19.6m budget (0.4%). Porth Cynnal: £390k overspend on £41.2m budget (0.9%)
findings.quote: Social care continues to face recruitment challenges, despite the Council's terms and conditions being relatively attractive. This is resulting in a continued need to use agency staff in frontline Social Worker roles and Care & Support roles in our Residential Care Homes. Within Porth Gofal there is a £352k net overspend for agency costs.

findings.headline: Out of county children's placements spiralling: £9.075m gross cost with 2 new placements since year-end and 4 at risk from provider closure.
findings.detail: The council spent £9.075m on 21 residential and 9 college placements, delivering a net £400k overspend after using £313k of reserves and a £1.332m budget movement. More critically, the paper flags that since year-end two new placements have been made and a South Wales provider has announced closure due to Welsh Government's 'Eliminating Profit' policy, affecting 4 more placements. The council has now transferred £2.0m to the Placements Equalisation reserve to absorb these pressures.
findings.matters: Out of county placements are a major cost driver and volatile. Continued growth in placements and the provider closure risk mean next year's budget is already under strain before it begins.
findings.figures: £9.075m gross expenditure; 21 residential placements + 9 college placements at year-end; 2 new placements post year-end; 4 placements at risk from provider closure; £2.0m transferred to equalisation reserve
findings.quote: At the end of Q4 there were 21 residential placements and 9 College placements. The final total gross expenditure in this area for 25/26 was £9.075m... However, since year-end, there have been 2 new placements and substantial changes to 2 existing placements. In addition, a private sector provider in South Wales has served advance notice of their intention to cease operations (due to the impact of the Welsh Government Eliminating Profit agenda) which will affect a further 4 existing placements.

findings.headline: Council explicitly acknowledges very challenging financial pressures alongside high service demands
findings.detail: Panel Performance Assessment explicitly describes the council as facing 'very challenging financial pressures' and 'high service demands'. Forward planning identifies social care and housing as ongoing priority monitoring areas for financial and service pressures.
findings.matters: Social care and housing are demand-led, high-cost service areas; their identification as pressure areas suggests structural budget strain in core services that will persist and require ongoing management.
findings.figures: Panel Performance Assessment report; social care and housing flagged in forward look governance priorities
findings.quote: Considering the current high service demands and very challenging financial pressures, Ceredigion County Council is a well-run local authority.

findings.headline: Council tax modelling increased to manage identified budget shortfalls in updated MTFS
findings.detail: The updated MTFS was designed to avoid creating wholly unrealistic budget shortfalls, but achieving this required increased underlying council tax modelling. This signals the council is relying on council tax revenue increases to manage structural budget gaps rather than finding savings.
findings.matters: Reliance on council tax increases to address budget shortfalls indicates constrained revenue sources and limited flexibility for the council to manage future financial stress without further council tax rises.
findings.figures: Council tax modelling increased in MTFS approved 23 October 2025
findings.quote: The MTFS therefore does not create a wholly unrealistic or unachievable Budget Shortfall, however in doing so there is an increase in the underlying Council Tax modelling.

findings.headline: Audit Wales found council lacked long-term financial strategy; council responded by updating MTFS
findings.detail: Audit Wales in November 2024 concluded the council lacked a long-term strategy for financial sustainability. The council responded by updating its MTFS to a 5-year horizon (2026/27-2030/31) and securing Full Council approval in October 2025. While the response was appropriate, it indicates the council was reactive rather than proactive on financial strategy.
findings.matters: An external audit finding of insufficient long-term financial strategy, even when addressed, indicates the council was behind on financial planning maturity and had to catch up, which is relevant to lender assessment of forward financial management.
findings.figures: MTFS extended to 5 years (2026/27-2030/31); updated and approved Full Council 23 October 2025
findings.quote: Audit Wales concluded that, overall, "The Council has arrangements in place to support its present financial sustainability but lacks a long-term strategy to support this."

findings.headline: Staff pay awards for 26/27 not yet determined; budget assumes c£4.1m but carries crystallisation risk
findings.detail: The budget incorporates c£4.1m for pay awards (included in £9.3m total cost pressures). However, awards are not yet set—determined by Welsh Government for teachers and UK Local Government Employers for other staff. The paper notes 'a level of budget risk until these crystalise' but confirms a contingency is held.
findings.matters: If actual pay awards exceed the £4.1m assumption or contingency, the council faces unplanned overspend unless additional savings are found mid-year.
findings.figures: c£4.1m assumed pay cost within £9.3m total cost pressures; pay awards not yet determined
findings.quote: Staff Pay awards are yet to be determined for 26/27, therefore there is a level of budget risk until these crystalise, but a contingency is held to assist in mitigating this risk.

findings.headline: S151 officer flags General Balances declining as percentage of budget and requiring proactive management, despite currently being adequate
findings.detail: General Balances are £7m (within the planned 3-5% range) and confirmed as adequate for 26/27. However, the S151 officer explicitly notes that with revenue budget increasing and balances static, the percentage will naturally decline and 'this will need to be proactively managed'.
findings.matters: Flagging the need for proactive management signals the S151 officer expects reserves will move toward inadequacy unless deliberate action is taken to replenish them.
findings.figures: General Balances £7.0m; planned range 3-5% of budget; estimated position at 31/03/27 earmarked reserves higher than pre-COVID baseline of c£20m
findings.quote: The impact of an increasing revenue budget, combined with relatively static General Balances, means that the %age naturally declines over a period of time, so this will need to be proactively managed.

findings.headline: Council committing £1m annually in recurring revenue funding to match capital grants, a new burden to unlock external funding
findings.detail: The budget dedicates £1m of revenue as recurring funding to provide match funding for priority capital schemes including Aberystwyth Coastal Defence, Lampeter vocational training, and school strategic outline programme projects. This is explicitly identified as a new investment to enable grant drawdown.
findings.matters: Revenue funding diverted to capital match funding reduces what is available for current services; it signals that external capital funding increasingly requires council revenue subsidy to access.
findings.figures: £1m recurring allocation; projects: Aberystwyth Coastal Defence, Lampeter vocational training, Aberaeron Primary, Rhydypennau Primary, Penparc Primary
findings.quote: £1m of recurring funding to be set aside to start providing match funding for key upcoming Capital projects e.g. Aberystwyth Coastal Defence scheme, Agricultural vocational training provision in Lampeter and wider Lampeter campus aspirations

findings.headline: Core capital funding has declined in real terms: £6.6m budgeted for 26/27 is lower in cash than the £7m received in 2008/09
findings.detail: Ceredigion is receiving only c£100k increase in core capital funding for 26/27. This continues a multi-year erosion of capital investment capacity, with the council's current core funding level below what it received 17 years ago in absolute cash terms.
findings.matters: Declining capital funding constrains infrastructure renewal capacity and increases reliance on external borrowing, grant-matching, or revenue subsidy to fund necessary capital programmes.
findings.figures: £6.6m core capital funding 26/27; £7m received 2008/09; £100k increase; £32m 26/27 capital programme; £99m multi-year (25/26-28/29)
findings.quote: The level of core capital funding (now £6.6m for 26/27) is still lower in cash terms than that received 17 years ago back in 2008/09 of £7m.

findings.headline: Auditor recommends significant improvement to external valuation contract management
findings.detail: The auditor raised a medium-priority recommendation that the Council's arrangements to monitor the external valuation contract need substantial improvement. The delivery issues directly caused the late accounts and the material misstatement.
findings.matters: Weak contract management over critical external services indicates control deficiencies affecting both the reliability of financial reporting and timely account production.
findings.figures: One medium-priority recommendation
findings.quote: The Council's arrangements to monitor the delivery of their asset valuations via an external contract could be significantly improved. The delivery issues experienced in year led to the delay in the preparation of the financial statements and contributed to a material misstatement in the draft accounts.

findings.headline: Accounts submitted 16 days late due to external valuer delivery failures
findings.detail: The Council missed the 30 June 2025 submission deadline, submitting accounts on 16 July 2025. The delay was directly caused by the external valuer delivering revaluation information late, incomplete, and in a format incompatible with the Council's asset management system, which reduced time available for finance officers to prepare the accounts.
findings.matters: Late submission indicates financial reporting process weaknesses. A lender would be concerned about the Council's ability to meet statutory reporting deadlines, particularly given pressure to bring forward future deadlines to 30 September.
findings.figures: 16 days late; deadline 30 June 2025, submission 16 July 2025
findings.quote: The accounts were submitted to us for audit 16 July 2025, which is just after the deadline of 30 June 2025... the initial revaluation information provided was not complete, later than expected and in a format that was not directly compatible for uploading to the Council's asset management system. This then significantly reduced the time available for finance officers

findings.headline: Repeated asset valuation failures: £25.7m misstatement now corrected, but third year running
findings.detail: The Council's asset valuations contained material errors for the third consecutive year. In 2024-25, a change in how schools were valued (as single units rather than blocks) caused a £25.710m overstatement of expenditure in the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement. The auditor also found Hafan Y Waun care home was valued on the wrong basis, overstating its value by £7.370m. Both errors were corrected, but the pattern is concerning.
findings.matters: Repeated valuation failures despite engaging an external valuer for the first time signal systemic weaknesses in the Council's asset management controls and financial reporting quality. A lender would view this pattern as a control deficiency.
findings.figures: £25.710 million overstatement; £7.370 million overstatement
findings.quote: In 2022-23 and 2023-24, we reported issues with the Council's valuation of land and buildings... a change in the valuation process for schools as one unit rather than several 'blocks' resulted in a significant error in their accounting treatment... This did not impact on the overall asset valuations but did result in an overstatement of £25.710 million in expenditure

news_drafts.headline: Ceredigion audit finds and corrects £17m asset error
news_drafts.lead: A miscalculation in the council's new asset valuation system overstated Ceredigion's assets by £17.078 million in 2025-26 — more than five times what auditors consider material — but the error was discovered during the audit process and corrected by management. The council also corrected a £478,706 error from double-counting of asset components. The council resolved delays from the previous year in the 2024-25 accounts, which were ultimately cleared by auditors. The 2025-26 accounts were submitted on time despite this year's significant errors being caught and corrected during audit. The council's internal auditor gave high assurance that governance and internal controls are sound, with no significant corporate concerns. However, Audit Wales recommended the council develop a longer-term financial strategy beyond its current medium-term plan to 2030-31.

news_drafts.headline: Ceredigion puts five-year financial strategy in place after audit criticism
news_drafts.lead: Ceredigion County Council has approved a five-year medium-term financial strategy (a formal plan setting out how it will balance spending and income) in response to Audit Wales criticism that it lacked a long-term plan. In November 2024, auditors found the council was financially sustainable but had no long-term strategy. The council approved an updated strategy in October 2025, covering 2026-27 to 2030-31, which places it on "a sounder medium to long term footing". The strategy acknowledges a budget shortfall that will be managed partly through increases in council tax. Since approval, the council has downgraded its top financial risk from 25 to 20.
